Adult Hardenberg, Stolephorus insularis, typically achieve a maximum recorded total length of 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], a modest size that positions them among the smaller members of the Engraulidae. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the embryonic development period is remarkably brief, with yolk-sac larvae emerging from the transparent, pelagic eggs after approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days]. The newly hatched prolarvae are minute, possessing a wet weight at birth of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value that underscores the lecithotrophic nature of the earliest life stages. This rapid initial development and diminutive starting mass are characteristic of a strategy that prioritizes a short, vulnerable egg phase in favor of a more protracted, feeding larval period in the plankton.

Sexual maturation in this anchovy species is attained at a relatively small body size. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 4.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.3 centimeters], a threshold that is reached several months after the completion of metamorphosis. Corresponding to this length, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 0.385 grams [Wwp = 0.385 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from local populations. This pubertal weight is less than one-seventh of the ultimate wet weight observed in fully-grown adults, which can reach up to 2.72 grams [Wwi = up to 2.72 grams]. The considerable scope for continued somatic growth after the initiation of reproductive activity suggests that individuals allocate resources to both length increase and gamete production concurrently during their early adult phase.

Reproductive output in Stolephorus insularis is characterized by frequent, low-event fecundity, a pattern typical of many small, short-lived clupeiforms. Under the warm thermal regime typical of its tropical habitat, averaging 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], ripe females appear capable of spawning daily, yielding approximately 360 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 360 eggs per year]. This constant, high-volume output is sustained by a rapid oocyte maturation cycle and is not channeled into a small number of large, seasonal clutches, but rather into a continuous release of pelagic eggs into the water column.

The species exhibits a comparatively short life history, a syndrome consistent with its small body size and high reproductive investment. In populations experiencing sustained water temperatures around 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the maximum lifespan has been documented at approximately 620 days [am = approximately 620 days], a duration that corresponds to less than two years from the moment of egg fertilisation. This abbreviated longevity means that most individuals complete their entire lives within a single annual cycle, engaging in a rapid growth phase, a pubertal transition at a small size, and an intensive, multi-month spawning period before succumbing to senescence. The maximum reproductive rate is bolstered by this compressed schedule, maximizing output during the relatively brief adult window.

Comparing the length-based transitions reveals a life history finely tuned to its pelagic environment. The species shifts from a larval to a juvenile body plan at a length well below the 4.3 centimeters [Lp = 4.3 centimeters] marker for puberty. Following this maturation event, individuals continue expanding their length toward the ultimate total length of 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], an asymptotic ceiling that constrains the maximum dimensions of the body cavity and thus the potential for egg batch size. The wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] is minute, a reflection of the small egg diameter. These tightly coupled traits—a brief embryonic phase, an early onset of reproduction, and a compressed lifespan—position Stolephorus insularis as a classic example of a fast-lived, capital-poor strategist thriving in the productive, warm waters of its range.
